steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on AXNav, a system that uses an LLM to turn natural-language manual accessibility test instructions into replayable tests on mobile apps. Cover why accessibility testing is still mostly manual, what AXNav does, related LLM work, and our contributions (formative study, system, user study).

steps.text:
- Accessibility support in mobile apps and the state of testing
- Cost of manual testing; formative study findings
- Our approach: natural language test instructions -> AXNav
- Motivation from prior LLM work
- Contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Many mobile apps still have incomplete support for accessibility features. Developers of these apps may not implement or test accessibility support because they lack awareness, organizational support, or experience in accessibility testing. For apps that do support accessibility features, developers often work together with experienced accessibility quality assurance (QA) testers. People in both roles may use automated tools like accessibility scanners, linters, and test automation to run UI test scenarios. But even though there are many tools available, most accessibility testing is still done manually. Part of the reason may be limitations of the tools themselves. For example, UI tests can be brittle or they don't exist at all, and scanners can give false positives. Also, manual testing can find issues that automated techniques alone cannot detect.

But manually testing all the possible accessibility scenarios and features is costly and hard to scale. We did a formative study with six accessibility QA testers and found that they often had trouble keeping up with the scope of apps and features they were assigned to test. Because of this testers limit the scope of their tests, which can let bugs slip through, and test instructions can become outdated. Research has addressed some of these challenges with automation, but there are still manual costs for writing and recording tests to be replayed. Recorded tests often have to be updated when the UI or navigation flow changes, the same as UI automation tests, which have to specify every step in the navigation flow in code.

- AXNav
  - natural language instructions specify accessibility testing steps; manual test instructions common, large databases
  - interprets instructions -> concrete actions, adapts as interface evolves
  - live cloud device, enables/configures accessibility features, heuristics flag issues
  - output: chaptered, annotated video with interaction trace + heuristic results
- Prior LLM work: recreate bug reports, test GUIs, automate web tasks; AXNav first for accessibility testing / controlling accessibility services and settings
- Contributions
  - formative study (6 testers)
  - AXNav system: LLM + pixel-based UI element detection; flags issues (non-increasing text, loops) for Dynamic Text, VoiceOver; replays via accessibility services
  - user study (10 testers)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Many mobile apps still have incomplete support for accessibility features. Developers of these apps may not implement or test accessibility support because they lack awareness, organizational support, or experience in accessibility testing. For apps that do support accessibility features, developers often work together with experienced accessibility quality assurance (QA) testers. People in both roles may use automated tools like accessibility scanners, linters, and test automation to run UI test scenarios. But even though there are many tools available, most accessibility testing is still done manually. Part of the reason may be limitations of the tools themselves. For example, UI tests can be brittle or they don't exist at all, and scanners can give false positives. Also, manual testing can find issues that automated techniques alone cannot detect.

But manually testing all the possible accessibility scenarios and features is costly and hard to scale. We did a formative study with six accessibility QA testers and found that they often had trouble keeping up with the scope of apps and features they were assigned to test. Because of this testers limit the scope of their tests, which can let bugs slip through, and test instructions can become outdated. Research has addressed some of these challenges with automation, but there are still manual costs for writing and recording tests to be replayed. Recorded tests often have to be updated when the UI or navigation flow changes, the same as UI automation tests, which have to specify every step in the navigation flow in code.

To address some of these challenges and to support the existing manual testing workflows of accessibility QA testers, we explore using natural language instructions to specify accessibility testing steps to a system. Manual test instructions are common artifacts in organizations, which often have large databases of manual steps for QA testers. Our system, AXNav, interprets natural language test instructions and produces a set of concrete actions that can be taken in an app, and then it adapts them automatically when the interface evolves. AXNav executes the actions on a live cloud device, enables and configures accessibility features as needed, and runs heuristics on the target screens to flag potential issues for manual testers. The output of AXNav is a chaptered, annotated video that captures the interaction trace and the heuristic results.

Our approach is motivated by prior work using Large Language Models (LLMs) to recreate bug reports, test GUIs, and automate tasks for web interfaces. As far as we know, AXNav is the first work to use LLMs for accessibility testing, or for controlling accessibility services and settings.

The contributions of this work are:

- A formative study with 6 professional QA and accessibility testers that shows the motivation and design considerations for a system supporting accessibility testing through manual tests based on natural language instructions.

- A novel system, AXNav, which converts manual accessibility test instructions into replayable, navigable videos using a large language model and a pixel-based UI element detection model. The system helps testers find potential issues (e.g., non-increasing text, loops) with multiple types of accessibility features (e.g., Dynamic Text, VoiceOver), and it replays tasks through accessibility services so testers can visualize and hear the task the way a user of the accessibility service might do it.

- A user study with 10 professional QA and accessibility testers that shows key insights into how accessibility testers might use natural language-based automation in their manual testing workflow.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Many mobile apps still have incomplete support for accessibility features [1,2,3,4,5]. Developers of these apps may not implement or test accessibility support due to a lack of awareness [4], organizational support [2,6], or experience in accessibility testing [6]. For apps that do support accessibility features, developers often work in tandem with experienced accessibility quality assurance (QA) testers [6]. Employees in both roles may use automated tools like accessibility scanners [7,8], linters [9], and test automation [10,11] to execute UI test scenarios. However, despite the many available tools, most accessibility testing is still done manually. This may partly be due to the limitations of the tools themselves: UI tests can be brittle [12,13] or non-existent [14,15,16], and scanners can provide false positives [17]. In addition, manual testing can reveal issues that automated techniques alone cannot detect [18].

However, manually testing all possible accessibility scenarios and features is costly and hard to scale. In a formative study with six accessibility QA testers, we found they often had difficulties keeping up with the scope of apps and features they were assigned to test. This causes testers to limit the scope of their tests, potentially letting bugs slip through, and can lead to outdated test instructions. While research has addressed some of these challenges through automation [19,20], there are still manual costs in writing and recording tests to be replayed. Recorded tests often need to be updated when the UI or navigation flow changes, similar to UI automation tests, which must specify each step in the navigation flow in code [13,12].

To address some of these challenges and support the existing manual testing workflows of accessibility QA testers, we explore using natural language instructions to specify accessibility testing steps to a system. Manual test instructions are common artifacts within organizations, which often have large databases of manual steps for QA testers. Our system, AXNav, interprets natural language test instructions to produce a set of concrete actions that can be taken in an app, and then adapts them automatically as the interface evolves. AXNav executes these actions on a live cloud device, enabling and configuring accessibility features as needed, and runs heuristics on target screens to flag potential issues to manual testers. AXNav's output is a chaptered, annotated video capturing the interaction trace along with heuristic results.

Our approach is motivated by prior work that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to recreate bug reports [21], test GUIs [22], and automate tasks for web interfaces [23]. To our knowledge, AXNav is the first work to use LLMs for accessibility testing, or for controlling accessibility services [24] and settings [25].

The contributions of this work are:

- A formative study with 6 professional QA and accessibility testers revealing the motivation and design considerations for a system to support accessibility testing through natural language instruction-based manual tests.

- A novel system, AXNav, that converts manual accessibility test instructions into replayable, navigable videos using a large language model and a pixel-based UI element detection model. The system helps testers pinpoint potential issues (e.g., non-increasing text, loops) with multiple types of accessibility features (e.g., Dynamic Text, VoiceOver) and replays tasks through accessibility services so that testers can visualize and hear the task as a user of the accessibility service might perform it.

- A user study with 10 professional QA and accessibility testers revealing key insights into how accessibility testers might use natural language-based automation within their manual testing workflow.
